compound.name: linalool
compound.one_liner: The floral-sweet alcohol that dominates Genovese-type basil oil; also a minor thyme oil constituent.

identity.note: Stereo-unspecified record; basil oils are usually reported as (-)-(R)-linalool (Duke lists '(-)-LINALOOL' rows) but the enantiomer record was not fetched.

occurrences.source_citation: Muráriková A, Ťažký A, Neugebauerová J, et al. (2017) Characterization of essential oil composition in different basil species and pot cultures by a GC-MS method. Molecules 22(7):1221
occurrences.database: Dr. Duke's Phytochemical and Ethnobotanical Databases
occurrences.note: Duke rows: LINALOOL Leaf Essent. Oil 14000-593000 ppm; Essential Oil 10-630000; Plant 5-8730 (Duke 1992). Paper: linalool quantified in all 7 cultivars, e.g. 'Ohře' 5.99 mg/mL, 'Red Rubin' 0.46 mg/mL (mg per mL of the analysed oil solution, GC-MS). Majdi 2020 also: linalool the major volatile in Cinnamon basil. | Basis as recorded: ppm as listed by Duke (basis not stated per row; for 'Essent. Oil' parts it is ppm of the oil, 10000 ppm = 1 %)

occurrences.source_citation: EMA/HMPC. Assessment report on Thymus vulgaris L., Thymus zygis L., herba. EMA/HMPC/342334/2013 (12 Nov 2013). https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/herbal-report/final-assessment-report-thymus-vulgaris-l-vulgaris-zygis-l-herba_en.pdf
occurrences.database: Dr. Duke's Phytochemical and Ethnobotanical Databases
occurrences.note: Duke: LINALOOL Essential Oil 28200-42800 ppm (2.8-4.3 % of oil); Plant 20-17420 ppm. EMA lists linalool among the main oil components and notes 'at least 6 chemotypes of Thymus vulgaris'; only the thymol type meets Ph. Eur. | Basis as recorded: ppm as listed by Duke (basis not stated per row; for 'Essent. Oil' parts it is ppm of the oil, 10000 ppm = 1 %) | RULING: EMA confirms ≥6 thyme chemotypes but no paper read names a linalool chemotype, so this row is verified:false.

processing_stability.volatility: steam-volatile: recovered in hydro/steam-distilled essential oil (see occurrence sources)
processing_stability.note: Solubility and heat-stability values not sourced in this pass.

compound.teaching_note: Linalool is why a sweet basil smells 'basil' rather than aniseed: the ratio of linalool to estragole and methyleugenol defines the basil chemotypes grown in the greenhouse, and it differs cultivar by cultivar [18].
gaps: Pharmacology, absorption and safety not researched in this pass.
No human evidence for the isolated compound found in this pass.
Enantiomer in basil (reported as (-)-(R)) not confirmed from a primary record.
Thyme linalool chemotype not named by a paper read; thyme row kept verified:false.
